life: Born in the French-Canadian farm settlement at Lake Gervais, he went back to Quebec's Beauce to marry and then north to the sawmill town of Knife Falls (Cloquet). He may have followed work where it was: in 1910 he boarded at Deerwood, on the new Cuyuna iron range, while Alfonsina kept house in Cloquet, and he ended his life in the logging country of Koochiching County.

life: A Cloquet man from boyhood to death, in a town that lived on its sawmills and the Northwest Paper Company. He was 24 and registered in Carlton County for the WWI draft when the fire of 12 October 1918 burned the city almost flat; he was in Cloquet in 1910 and again, married, in January 1920, so the family tradition that they lived through the fire there fits the record.
life_basis: sourced (residences) / family tradition (presence on the day of the fire)

events.text: 12 October: fires set by locomotive sparks sweep Carlton and St. Louis counties; over 450 die across the region but only five in Cloquet, as the mayor's four evacuation trains carry more than 7,000 people out; the city burns almost flat. Left standing: three of five sawmills, one school, scattered houses, and the buildings along St. Louis Avenue on Dunlap Island

places.name: Northeastern Hotel, 115 St. Louis Ave, Dunlap Island, Cloquet

life: Born a year and five days after the fire, into a town still rebuilding. Family tradition says she was born in a hotel bar on an island in Cloquet, "because it was the only thing that survived the fire." One building matches: the Northeastern Hotel, a two-story brick hotel with a 30-foot mahogany bar on Dunlap Island, which survived and served as a hospital after the fire. It was not literally the only survivor, and no record has been read that places her birth there.
